summary: This informational RFC provides guidelines for developing an interactive audio codec in the IETF, covering the process, evaluation, requirements conformance, and intellectual property.

eli5.summary: Rules of the road for a group that wants to design a new way to compress sound, from how to test it to how to handle patents.

questions: how does the ietf develop a codec
how does ietf develop audio codecs
what is the ietf codec process
subtitle: How the IETF develops interactive audio codecs in the open.

tldr.problem: Developing an audio codec requires coordinating technical work, intellectual property, testing and implementation across the IETF community without getting entangled in patent issues.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6569 describes a nine-step process that starts with requirements, moves through codec proposals and consolidation, iterative improvement of a baseline codec, parallel testing, and ends with a final specification and testing report.
tldr.outcome: The IETF codec working group now has a documented framework to develop unencumbered codecs that can be freely implemented and distributed. The process has been used by subsequent codec projects.

facts.label: Development steps
facts.value: Nine stages from requirements to final specification

facts.label: Test methodologies
facts.value: PESQ, PEAQ, MUSHRA, real-world distributed testing

facts.label: Implementation requirement
facts.value: Normative software reference implementation required in RFC

today: RFC 6569 remains an Informational document that guides codec development in the IETF. The process described has been applied to subsequent IETF codec work, and the principles of open development, IP disclosure, and widespread implementation continue to be important values in IETF standards development.

sections.title: Why the IETF Needs Codec Guidelines
sections.content: Developing an interactive audio codec that works across the Internet requires coordination among many organizations and standards bodies. The RFC explains that the IETF wants to create codecs that can be widely implemented and freely distributed among application developers, service operators, and end users. This is different from many existing codecs that come with licensing restrictions or patent encumbrances that limit who can use them.
sections.eli5: The IETF wants to make a free sound compressor that anyone can use without paying royalties.

sections.title: The Nine-Step Development Process
sections.content: The process outlined in the RFC proceeds in nine stages. First, the community identifies requirements through an Internet-Draft. Second, parties interested in contributing propose existing or new codecs. Third, intellectual property disclosures are made early and transparently. Fourth, the requirements document is refined based on what proposals show is achievable. Fifth, the working group evaluates the strengths, weaknesses and innovative aspects of contributed codecs. Sixth, interested parties collaborate to combine the best ideas from contributions into a consolidated codec. Seventh, participants iteratively improve the baseline codec's individual components: predictors, transforms, quantizers, entropy coders. Eighth, in parallel with implementation work, developers perform evaluation using metrics like Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) and Perceptual Evaluation of Audio Quality (PEAQ), and real-world testing. Ninth, the group produces a testing results document that captures testing before stabilization, after stabilization, and after RFC publication.
sections.eli5: First decide what you need, then collect ideas. Check for patent problems early. Combine the best ideas into one design. Keep improving each piece. Test it constantly. Write down what you learned.

sections.title: Evaluation and Testing
sections.content: The RFC emphasizes that lab evaluation should happen throughout development because it ensures progress toward meeting requirements. For minor changes, objective measurements such as PESQ, PEAQ, and signal-to-noise ratio validated by informal subjective testing are usually sufficient. For more complex changes or controversial issues, the working group should perform internal testing using established methodologies such as MUSHRA (Multiple Stimuli with Hidden Reference and Anchor). The RFC also emphasizes the importance of distributed real-world testing through the Internet community, allowing people with different equipment and use cases to test the codec. The final characterization must be based on the reference implementation only, and the RFC notes that the IETF does not have its own testing resources, so it relies on volunteers.
sections.eli5: Keep measuring how well it works. Ask people to rate decoded sound samples. Let internet users test it too. At the end, have independent labs test the final version.

sections.title: Specification Guidelines
sections.content: When specifying a codec, the RFC provides eight key guidelines. First, the codec must include a normative software implementation in the RFC, used to verify conformance. Second, bugs found after publication are handled through an errata list, though a public repository is desirable. Third, the number of normative (RFC 2119 keyword) requirements should be minimized to allow interoperable but diverse implementations. Fourth, to avoid bias toward certain architectures, the decoder specification should not require bit-exact conformance. Fifth, decoder-side-only error concealment (packet loss concealment) does not need specification. Sixth, encoders need not use all bitstream features, but decoders must handle all combinations. Seventh, compressed test vectors must be provided to verify conformance. Eighth, objective measurement targets for encoders are recommended.
sections.eli5: Include working code in the RFC. Write down the rules clearly but not too strictly. The decoder has to follow the rules exactly; the encoder can vary. Provide test examples.

sections.title: Patent and IP Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that producing an unencumbered codec is desirable because licensing and royalties make it difficult for small development teams to implement and distribute multimedia applications. The working group prefers technologies with no known intellectual property claims, or if claims exist, an offer of royalty-free licensing. The RFC cites four reasons: application developers find encumbrances difficult to work with; small teams cannot afford usage-based licensing; many software is now distributed freely; and open-source projects typically cannot accept restricted licenses. The working group commits to following BCP 79, which states that the IETF generally prefers technologies with no IPR claims or royalty-free licensing. Contributors must disclose IPR early under BCP 79. If no royalty-free license can be obtained for a patent, the working group should consider alternative algorithms. The RFC also notes that the source code for the reference implementation must be made available under a BSD-style license.
sections.eli5: Try to avoid patents. If patents are involved, make sure the license is free for everyone, forever, with no royalties.

sections.title: Coordination with Other Standards Bodies
sections.content: The RFC acknowledges that other standards development organizations (SDOs) such as ITU-T, MPEG, ETSI, 3GPP and 3GPP2 also work on codec development and standardization. The RFC states that to avoid uncoordinated protocol development (as discussed in RFC 5704), the IETF must maintain design authority for its codec. The RFC notes two possible outcomes: the IETF can adopt an existing codec from another SDO and call it the IETF codec, with ownership remaining with the original SDO; or the IETF can produce a new codec, which becomes an IETF specification under complete IETF control, separate from any original SDO's evolution. The RFC also notes that IETF participants can include people who work in other SDOs, and that other SDOs can contribute expertise, characterization and evaluation techniques, or provide input through liaison statements.
sections.eli5: Other organizations might make codecs too. The IETF keeps its codec independent and under its own control. But we can listen to ideas from other groups.
